cards.front: A macrophage internalizes about 3% of its surface membrane each minute without shrinking. Roughly how long does it take to internalize an area equal to its entire surface, and why does the cell not shrink?
cards.back: 100% / (3% per min) ≈ 33.3 minutes (roughly half an hour). The cell does not shrink because membrane returns to the surface just as fast as it is pulled in.
cards.quote: A macrophage pulls in about 3 percent of its surface membrane each minute—its whole surface roughly every half hour—without shrinking.

cards.front: Why must cells import blood cholesterol (LDL) and transferrin-bound iron by receptor-mediated endocytosis rather than membrane channels or carriers?
cards.back: LDL particles are far too large to pass through channels or carriers, so surface receptors bind them and carry them inside within pinched-off membrane vesicles.
cards.quote: Blood cholesterol rides in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles, far too large for channels or carriers.
cards.section: What's endocytosis used for?

cards.front: How does endocytosis contribute to plasma membrane upkeep?
cards.back: It takes back the extra membrane added to the surface by secretion and pulls worn membrane proteins inward for disposal.
cards.quote: Secretion adds membrane to the surface and endocytosis takes it back, pulling worn membrane proteins in for disposal.
cards.section: What's endocytosis used for?

cards.front: What two opposite effects can endocytosis have on a receptor's signal, and when is the outcome mostly decided?
cards.back: It can end the signal by removing and destroying the receptor, or move the active receptor to an intracellular platform to keep signaling or signal differently—decided mostly after uptake.
cards.quote: Endocytosis can end a signal by removing and destroying the receptor, or move it to an intracellular platform where the active receptor keeps signaling or signals differently—decided mostly after uptake.
cards.section: What's endocytosis used for?

cards.front: Early endosomes sort internalized receptors, returning untagged ones to the surface; active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside {{c1::internal vesicles}}.
cards.why: Sealing encloses the receptor's cytoplasmic tail away from cytosolic signaling partners.
cards.quote: Early endosomes sort internalized receptors, returning untagged ones to the surface; active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.
cards.section: What's endocytosis used for?

cards.front: Why are adaptor proteins such as AP2 required in a clathrin-coated pit, and what three components does AP2 bind?
cards.back: Clathrin touches neither the membrane nor cargo, so adaptors bridge them. AP2 binds the plasma-membrane lipid PIP2, short cytoplasmic receptor tail sequences, and clathrin.
cards.why: Some receptors instead enter by binding a linker such as arrestin.
cards.quote: Clathrin touches neither membrane nor cargo; adaptor proteins bridge them. The main plasma-membrane adaptor, AP2, binds the lipid PIP2 (from the lesson on lipid anchors), short tail sequences, and clathrin.
cards.section: Getting inside: a coat, a reader, and a cut

cards.front: In cells from patient J.D., a tyrosine-to-cysteine mutation in the LDL receptor's cytoplasmic tail allows LDL binding but blocks uptake. Where do ferritin-labeled LDL dots appear under electron microscopy compared with normal cells, and what does this show?
cards.back: Normal cells cluster the dark LDL dots inside coated pits, whereas J.D.'s cells leave them scattered across flat membrane outside pits. This shows that entry requires an adaptor-readable signal in the receptor's cytoplasmic tail.
cards.quote: Normal cells cluster the dots inside coated pits; J.D.'s cells leave them scattered across flat membrane outside pits, showing that entry requires an adaptor-readable signal in the receptor tail.
cards.section: Getting inside: a coat, a reader, and a cut

cards.front: When a clathrin-coated pit hangs by a thin neck, the large GTPase {{c1::dynamin}} forms a collar around it and hydrolyzes GTP to cut the vesicle free.
cards.why: After fission, the clathrin coat strips off so the bare vesicle can fuse.
cards.quote: When the pit hangs by a thin neck, dynamin—a large GTPase—forms a collar around it and hydrolyzes GTP to cut the vesicle free
cards.section: Getting inside: a coat, a reader, and a cut

cards.front: A drug blocks removal of the clathrin coat immediately after a coated vesicle is cut free from the plasma membrane. What happens to delivery of its cargo to early endosomes, and why?
cards.back: Cargo delivery stalls because the coated vesicle cannot fuse with the early endosome. The coat must strip off after fission so the bare vesicle membrane can fuse.
cards.quote: the coat then strips off so the bare vesicle can fuse.
cards.section: Getting inside: a coat, a reader, and a cut

cards.front: Besides clathrin-coated pits, what other endocytic entry routes do cells use?
cards.back: Caveolae (flask-shaped pits built around caveolin), macropinocytosis (gulping fluid), and less-mapped clathrin-independent routes.
cards.quote: Other doors exist: caveolae (flask-shaped pits built around caveolin), macropinocytosis (gulping fluid), and less-mapped clathrin-independent routes.
cards.section: Getting inside: a coat, a reader, and a cut

cards.front: When plasma membrane folds inward to form an early endosome, which way do a transmembrane receptor's ligand-binding end and cytoplasmic tail face?
cards.back: The ligand-binding end faces the interior fluid (lumen), while the cytoplasmic tail still points into the cytosol.
cards.quote: Folding membrane inward leaves the ligand-binding end facing the interior fluid (lumen) and the cytoplasmic tail still pointing into the cytosol.
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: A proton pump holds the early endosome lumen near {{c1::pH 6 to 6.5}} (three- to tenfold more protons than pH 7), releasing many ligands from their receptors.
cards.why: In this mild acid, LDL falls off its receptor and iron falls off transferrin.
cards.quote: A proton pump holds the lumen near pH 6 to 6.5 (three- to tenfold more protons than pH 7), releasing many ligands
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: A proton-pump inhibitor raises early endosome lumen pH to about 7 without blocking LDL receptor synthesis or coated-pit entry. What happens to LDL uptake over the next few hours, and why?
cards.back: LDL uptake falls sharply. Without mild acid (pH 6 to 6.5), LDL cannot detach from its receptor in the early endosome, so receptors cannot recycle empty to pick up additional particles.
cards.why: Normally an LDL receptor completes a recycling round trip roughly every ten minutes.
cards.quote: releasing many ligands: LDL falls off its receptor, and iron falls off transferrin.
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: How does the tubular shape of an early endosome separate untagged membrane receptors from dissolved luminal cargo?
cards.back: Thin tubules have far more membrane per unit volume than the round body, so untagged membrane proteins diffuse into the tubules while dissolved cargo stays mostly in the round body.
cards.quote: Untagged membrane proteins diffuse into the tubules while dissolved cargo stays mostly in the round body.
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: An early endosome consists of a spherical body of radius R (surface-to-volume ratio 3/R) and a thin cylindrical tubule of radius r = R/10 (surface-to-volume ratio 2/r). How many times more membrane per unit volume does the tubule hold, and what percentage of the sphere's fluid does equal membrane enclose?
cards.back: Ratio = (2 / (R/10)) / (3 / R) = (20/R) / (3/R) = 20/3 ≈ 6.7 (nearly seven times more membrane per unit volume). Equal membrane therefore encloses 3/20 = 15% of the sphere's fluid.
cards.quote: A tubule with one-tenth the radius of the round body holds nearly seven times more membrane per unit volume—so equal membrane encloses only ~15% of the sphere's fluid.
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: At pH 6 inside an early endosome, Ligand A detaches from its receptor while Ligand B stays tightly bound. Neither receptor carries ubiquitin, and both drift into thin tubules. Where do Ligand A and Ligand B end up, and why?
cards.back: Ligand B rides back to the surface attached to its receptor in the tubule membrane, while freed Ligand A stays mostly in the fluid-filled round body. Bound ligand partitions with the membrane, whereas dissolved ligand stays in the bulk fluid.
cards.quote: Ligand B rides back to the surface attached to its receptor in the tubule membrane, because it is held in membrane rather than dissolved
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: Which Rab GTPases mediate rapid versus slower receptor recycling from early endosomes, and on what timescales?
cards.back: Rab4 drives rapid recycling (a few minutes), whereas Rab4 and Rab11 drive slower recycling through a second compartment (tens of minutes).
cards.why: An LDL receptor makes its round trip roughly every ten minutes.
cards.quote: pinched-off tubules recycle receptors rapidly via Rab4 (a few minutes) or more slowly through a second compartment via Rab4 and Rab11 (tens of minutes).
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: How do Rab GTPases label endosomal compartments and control trafficking steps?
cards.back: In their active GTP-bound state (flipped by GEFs and GAPs), Rabs sit on a specific compartment membrane and recruit effectors that tether incoming vesicles and help them fuse.
cards.why: Human cells have more than sixty Rabs marking compartments, domains, or traffic steps.
cards.quote: in its GTP form it sits on the membrane and recruits effectors, proteins that bind only the on state, which tether incoming vesicles and help them fuse.
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: The small GTPase {{c1::Rab5}} marks the early endosome and, in its GTP form, recruits effectors that tether and fuse incoming vesicles.
cards.quote: Rab5 marks the early endosome; in its GTP form it sits on the membrane and recruits effectors
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: A cell expresses a mutant Rab5 that binds GTP normally but cannot hydrolyze it to GDP. What happens to early endosomes, and why?
cards.back: Early endosomes fuse too often and grow large. Locked in the active GTP-bound state, mutant Rab5 remains on the membrane and continuously recruits effectors that tether and fuse incoming vesicles.
cards.quote: Rabs are small GTPase switches (on with GTP, off with GDP, flipped by GEFs and GAPs, from the lesson on GTPase switches).
cards.section: The early endosome is a sorting station

cards.front: How does ubiquitin tagging on an active endosomal receptor such as EGFR differ in destination from standard proteasomal targeting?
cards.back: Rather than targeting the proteasome, endosomal ubiquitin (added to active EGFR by Cbl) is bound by ESCRT, diverting the receptor into internal vesicles toward the lysosome.
cards.quote: Rather than targeting the proteasome, endosomal ubiquitin is bound by ESCRT, which gathers tagged receptors and pushes the patch inward (away from the cytosol) into internal vesicles
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: Endosomal ubiquitin is bound by {{c1::ESCRT}}, which gathers tagged receptors and pushes the membrane patch inward into internal vesicles, forming a multivesicular endosome.
cards.why: A multivesicular endosome (MVE) is also called a multivesicular body.
cards.quote: endosomal ubiquitin is bound by ESCRT, which gathers tagged receptors and pushes the patch inward (away from the cytosol) into internal vesicles, forming a multivesicular endosome (MVE)
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: Why does moving a ubiquitin-tagged receptor into an internal endosomal vesicle silence its signal even before lysosomal digestion begins?
cards.back: Sealing encloses the receptor's cytoplasmic tail inside the internal vesicle, cutting it off from cytosolic signaling partners while placing the whole receptor inside for lysosomal enzymes.
cards.quote: Sealing the receptor inside an internal vesicle cuts its cytoplasmic tail off from cytosolic partners—ending the signal before digestion—and places the whole receptor inside for lysosomal enzymes.
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: A cell overproduces an endosomal deubiquitinating enzyme that strips ubiquitin from active EGF receptors on early endosomes. How do receptor destination and signaling duration change, and why?
cards.back: Most likely, the receptors stay on the outer membrane, recycle to the surface, and signal longer instead of entering lysosomes. Because sorting is a reversible competition until sealing completes, losing ubiquitin prevents ESCRT from sequestering them into internal vesicles.
cards.quote: Most likely, without ubiquitin ESCRT does not sequester them into internal vesicles; they stay on the outer membrane, recycle to the surface, and signal longer instead of entering lysosomes.
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: How did Marino Zerial's laboratory obtain live-cell evidence for Rab conversion during endosome maturation?
cards.back: They filmed single endosomes in living cells and watched Rab5 leave the membrane as Rab7 arrived.
cards.quote: Meanwhile, Marino Zerial's laboratory filmed single endosomes in living cells and watched Rab5 leave as Rab7 arrived (Rab conversion).
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: As an early endosome matures toward a lysosome, Rab5 leaves and {{c1::Rab7}} arrives, bringing new effectors, stronger acid, and more internal vesicles.
cards.quote: With Rab7 come new effectors, stronger acid (~pH 5.5 in late endosomes), and more internal vesicles, before fusion with a lysosome
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: How does lumenal pH change as cargo moves from an early endosome to a late endosome and then a lysosome?
cards.back: It becomes progressively more acidic: pH 6 to 6.5 in early endosomes, about pH 5.5 in late endosomes, and pH 4.5 to 5 in lysosomes.
cards.quote: stronger acid (~pH 5.5 in late endosomes), and more internal vesicles, before fusion with a lysosome (digestive enzymes at pH 4.5 to 5) breaks the receptor down.
cards.section: Headed to the lysosome: the receptor is sealed inside

cards.front: In 1996, Sandra Schmid's lab blocked EGF receptor uptake in HeLa cells using a dominant-negative dynamin mutant defective in GTP binding and hydrolysis. What split result did they observe, and why must it be interpreted cautiously?
cards.back: Cells divided more, yet full MAP kinase ERK activation fell, arguing that part of the EGF signal required uptake. Caution is needed because dynamin has other cellular effects, and later studies blocking uptake by other methods did not all see the same fall in ERK.
cards.quote: Instead, the result split: cells divided more, yet full ERK activation fell. That split argued that part of the EGF signal required uptake
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: After ligand binding, a receptor activates Pathway X and Pathway Y. Blocking endocytosis traps the active receptor at the plasma membrane; Pathway X stays normal, while Pathway Y falls sharply. What does this show about where each pathway originates?
cards.back: Pathway X is generated at the plasma membrane, whereas Pathway Y requires receptor internalization and is generated from endosomes. If endocytosis only terminated signals, both outputs would rise or persist.
cards.quote: Recall the second half of our rule: active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: How does Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) change its signaling output after moving from the plasma membrane to endosomes?
cards.back: At the plasma membrane TLR4 signals via MyD88, whereas on endosomes it signals via TRIF to switch on interferon genes.
cards.quote: Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) signals via MyD88 at the plasma membrane and via TRIF on endosomes to switch on interferon genes.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: Why do the nucleic-acid sensors TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9 signal only in endosomes?
cards.back: Endosomes are where internalized microbial remains arrive, exposing microbial nucleic acids to these receptors.
cards.quote: Nucleic-acid sensors TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9 work only in endosomes, where microbial remains arrive.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: A transmembrane receptor normally triggers Output 1 at the plasma membrane and Output 2 from early endosomes. A single point mutation in its cytoplasmic tail destroys its coated-pit adaptor signal without harming ligand binding or effector binding. Predict its surface distribution and both signaling outputs.
cards.back: The receptor remains scattered across flat plasma membrane instead of clustering in coated pits; Output 1 persists (or rises) at the surface, while Output 2 drops sharply. This rests on two rules: coated-pit entry requires an adaptor-readable cytoplasmic tail sequence, and endosomal outputs require receptor internalization.
cards.quote: Other receptors clearly change output upon uptake.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: Compare how two perturbations affect TLR4's endosomal TRIF (interferon-gene) output: (A) blocking endocytosis with a dominant-negative dynamin mutant versus (B) blocking ESCRT so internalized receptors cannot be sealed into internal vesicles.
cards.back: (A) Blocking dynamin decreases TRIF output because TLR4 cannot reach endosomes, while MyD88 continues at the surface. (B) If TLR4 is sorted by ESCRT like other active receptors (the lesson shows this for EGFR, not TLR4), blocking ESCRT would be expected to prolong TRIF output, because unsealed receptors keep their tails exposed to the cytosol. Rests on TLR4's endosomal TRIF signaling and the general rule that active receptors signal until sealed.
cards.quote: active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.
cards.section: What's endocytosis used for?

cards.front: In roughly 3% of non-small-cell lung cancers, how does exon 14 deletion in the RTK MET cause prolonged signaling without creating an intrinsically overactive kinase?
cards.back: Exon 14 deletion removes tyrosine 1003, the Cbl docking site. Poorly ubiquitinated, mutant MET escapes lysosomal destruction and keeps signaling longer than it should.
cards.why: Two MET kinase inhibitors, capmatinib and tepotinib, are approved for these tumors.
cards.quote: a splicing error deletes exon 14 from mRNA for the receptor tyrosine kinase MET, removing tyrosine 1003 (the Cbl docking site).
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: A mutant receptor tyrosine kinase in tumor cells binds ligand, autophosphorylates, and leaves the cell surface at the normal rate, yet carries almost no ubiquitin and has a sixfold longer half-life after ligand addition. Which step is most likely defective, and why does signaling persist?
cards.back: Sorting into internal endosomal vesicles (and lysosomal degradation) is defective. Without ubiquitin, the active receptor escapes sealing inside internal vesicles and keeps signaling from the outer endosome membrane or recycled surface pool.
cards.quote: Poorly ubiquitinated, mutant MET escapes the lysosome and keeps signaling for longer than it should—not an overactive kinase, just a receptor missing its turn.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: In a non-small-cell lung cancer driven by MET exon 14 deletion (loss of Tyr1003), predict whether an inhibitor of endosomal deubiquitinating enzymes or a MET kinase inhibitor (capmatinib or tepotinib) will curb mutant MET signaling, and why.
cards.back: A MET kinase inhibitor curbs signaling directly, whereas a deubiquitinating-enzyme inhibitor would not be expected to restore degradation. Because deleting Tyr1003 removes the Cbl docking site, mutant MET is barely ubiquitinated in the first place, leaving little ubiquitin to protect. Rests on the Cbl-docking, reversible ubiquitination, and MET kinase-inhibitor rules.
cards.quote: Two MET kinase inhibitors, capmatinib and tepotinib, are approved for these tumors.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: On each 10-minute endosomal pass, a wild-type receptor recycles 60% and degrades 40%, while a sorting mutant recycles 90% and degrades 10%. Starting from equal pools with no new synthesis, what fraction of each remains after 30 minutes (3 passes), and what is the mutant-to-wild-type survival ratio?
cards.back: Wild-type: 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.216 (21.6%). Mutant: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729 (72.9%). Ratio: 0.729 / 0.216 = 3.375 (about 3.4 times as many surviving mutant receptors).
cards.quote: Normal: 0.5 × 0.5 = 25%. Mutant: 0.9 × 0.9 = 81%—more than three times as many surviving receptors after just two passes.
cards.section: A receptor that keeps talking, and one that escapes

cards.front: Cells expressing EGF receptors are stimulated continuously with either EGF (which tends to stay bound in acidic endosomes) or transforming growth factor alpha (TGF-α, which lets go in mild acid). Predict how EGF receptor fate differs under the two ligands, and why.
cards.back: EGF tends to drive lysosomal destruction of the receptor, whereas TGF-α lets go in mild acid and the receptor recycles. Staying bound at endosomal pH keeps the receptor active and tends to send it for degradation, while dissociating in mild acid lets empty receptors return via tubules.
cards.quote: on the EGF receptor, EGF tends to stay bound in endosomes and drives lysosomal destruction, whereas transforming growth factor alpha lets go in mild acid and the receptor recycles.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Design two receptors on the same cell that bind ligand simultaneously: Receptor A must signal for ~10 minutes and then stay silent for hours; Receptor B must signal for hours. Using early-endosome sorting decisions, what ligand pH-sensitivity and tail features does each need?
cards.back: Receptor A needs a ligand that stays bound at pH 6, an activity-dependent ubiquitin-ligase docking site (such as a self-phosphorylated tail tyrosine), and lysines for tagging so ESCRT seals it into internal vesicles until new receptors are made. Receptor B needs no ligase site and a ligand that dissociates at pH 6 so empty receptors recycle in minutes via tubules.
cards.why: Adding a recycling-machinery tail motif—such as the PDZ-binding sequence at the end of the β2-adrenergic receptor—makes Receptor B's return even surer. Rests on acid-dissociation recycling and ESCRT sealing rules.
cards.quote: Give the brief receptor an activity-dependent ubiquitin-ligase docking site (such as a self-phosphorylated tail tyrosine), lysines for tagging, and a ligand that stays bound at pH 6
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A receptor makes an endosomal round trip every 10 minutes with no new synthesis. With Ligand X (stays bound at pH 6, driving degradation of 50% per pass) versus Ligand Y (dissociates at pH 6, allowing default recycling with only 10% degraded per pass), how many times more receptors survive after 40 minutes (4 passes) with Ligand Y than with Ligand X?
cards.back: Ligand X: 0.5⁴ = 0.0625 (6.25%). Ligand Y: 0.9⁴ = 0.6561 (65.61%). Ratio: 0.6561 / 0.0625 = 10.4976 (about 10.5 times more receptors survive). Rests on acid-dissociation recycling versus sustained ubiquitination-driven degradation compounding across each endosomal pass.
cards.quote: Give the lasting receptor no ligase site and a ligand that dissociates at pH 6. Empty receptors recycle via tubules in minutes to bind again
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Most Rab GTPases carry hydrophobic 20-carbon geranylgeranyl lipid tails that would stick to any membrane. How do GDI, a membrane displacement factor, and GEFs keep each Rab on its target membrane?
cards.back: Soluble GDI masks GDP-Rab's lipid tail until a membrane displacement factor releases it and a compartment-specific GEF switches it to GTP; GDI cannot extract GTP-Rab.
cards.why: The Rab therefore stays anchored on the membrane where its GEF sits until a GAP switches it back to GDP.
cards.quote: Later work points to each Rab's GEF as a main part of the address: a Rab is switched on, and so held, on the membrane where its GEF sits.
cards.section: How a Rab finds its membrane

cards.front: A cell is engineered so that Rab5's GEF localizes exclusively to the Golgi membrane rather than early endosomes, while GDI and GAPs remain normal. Predict where active Rab5 accumulates and how early-endosome fusion changes, and why.
cards.back: Active Rab5 accumulates on the Golgi membrane, and early-endosome tethering and fusion fall. Because GDI cannot remove GTP-Rab, Rab5 stays held where its GEF switches it on—away from early endosomes—depriving early endosomes of GTP-Rab5 effectors. Rests on the GEF membrane-address rule and Rab5 effector-recruitment rule.
cards.quote: GDI does not pull off the GTP form, so the Rab stays put until a GAP switches it off.
cards.section: How a Rab finds its membrane

cards.front: Late-endosome internal vesicles are rich in an unusual lipid, {{c1::lysobisphosphatidic acid}}, which is scarce in early endosomes.
cards.quote: Late-endosome internal vesicles are rich in an unusual lipid, lysobisphosphatidic acid, which is scarce in early endosomes.
cards.section: A lipid of late endosomes

cards.front: In HeLa cells studied by Sigismund, Di Fiore, and colleagues, how did low versus high EGF doses alter EGF receptor entry and fate, and what safe general conclusion follows?
cards.back: Low doses drove coated-pit uptake toward recycling; high doses added ubiquitin, shifted some uptake to a clathrin-independent route, and favored destruction. Safe conclusion: signaling strength can influence entry route and fate.
cards.why: Other labs see clathrin carrying most receptors at high doses too, so the specific route shift is treated as one cell line's result.
cards.quote: other labs see clathrin carrying most receptors at high doses too; the safe conclusion is that signaling strength can influence both entry route and fate.
cards.section: Dose and route for the EGF receptor
